title: parseFloat("1,234.56") is 1 - not 1234.56, not NaN
assumption: parseFloat on a reasonable-looking number string either parses the whole number correctly or fails loudly.

input.description: A price pasted from a spreadsheet, invoice, or a US-formatted input field ("$1,234.56") run through parseFloat to get a number.

what_goes_wrong: `parseFloat("1,234.56")` returns `1` - it silently stops at the first character it can't parse (the comma) and returns whatever valid number prefix it found, rather than parsing the full value or raising an error.
why: JavaScript's `parseFloat` is specified to skip leading whitespace, consume the longest prefix of the string that is valid decimal-literal syntax, and return that - it never looks at (or errors on) what comes after. A comma is not part of that syntax, so parsing stops right after the leading "1" and ",234.56" is silently discarded. A leading "$" is not number syntax either, so `parseFloat("$1,234.56")` finds no valid prefix at all and returns NaN. `Number()` is stricter - it requires the whole string to be numeric - so it returns NaN for both.

repros.expected_output: ValueError: could not convert string to float: '1,234.56'

fix: Never feed locale-formatted user input straight into parseFloat/float(). Strip grouping separators explicitly (knowing which character is the grouping separator for the input's locale) before parsing, or use a locale-aware parser (e.g. derive the separators from `Intl.NumberFormat(locale).formatToParts(1234.5)` in JS) rather than a generic numeric parser.

test_cases.note: A their_parse_price(input) function given US-formatted "1,234.56" should return 1234.56, not silently truncate to 1 like raw parseFloat/Number does.
